item.title: Every player from California to play for the Brooklyn Nets - Elden Campbell
item.description: The Brooklyn Nets have signed, drafted, and traded for players from virtually every state in the US, and much of the wider world beyond the United States. From Alabama to Wyoming, and from Australia to Ukraine, the Nets have a long and distinguished history of turning over every stone to find the talent needed to succeed in the NBA. From their start in the American Basketball Association (ABA) as the New Jersey Americans and New York Nets to their jump to the NBA as the New Jersey Nets right through to today, the organization has cast their net for talent wide since the inception of the ball club. For this installment of our series documenting the provenience of every Nets player to suit up for the franchise, let's take a look at every player from California who has played for Brooklyn. Our focus in this article is Elden Campbell. An alum of Clemson, he was picked up with the 27th overall selection of the 1990 NBA Draft by the Los Angeles Lakers. The Inglewood, California native played the first 9 seasons of his pro career with Los Angeles. He also played for the Charlotte Hornets , (then) New Orleans Hornets (now, Pelicans), Seattle SuperSonics, and the Detroit Pistons before he was claimed on waivers by the (then) New Jersey (now, Brooklyn) Nets in 2005. His stay with the team lasted until he signed with Detroit again later that spring. During his time suiting up for the Nets, Campbell put up 1.1 rebounds per game. item.title: Tigers respond to Gelof injury lawsuit in court. Here's what the team says
item.description: The Detroit Tigers and their co-defendants have responded in court to a lawsuit filed by Athletics third baseman Zack Gelof , arguing they cannot be held legally responsible for an injury he suffered during a July game at Comerica Park . Their motion, filed Oct. 29, contends that co-defendants Ilitch Holdings and the Detroit-Wayne County Stadium Authority did not control Comerica Park and therefore cannot be liable for its conditions. The stadium authority also claimed governmental immunity. The Tigers argue Gelof, as a professional baseball player, assumed the inherent risks of the game, including the possibility of colliding with the fence. They also contend the exposed fencing was "open and obvious," which should bar his claims. They are asking the court to dismiss the lawsuit. According to the lawsuit, filed Sept. 28 in Wayne County Circuit Court, Gelof was sliding to catch a foul ball along the left field line during a game against the Tigers when his right knee struck an exposed metal fence protruding into or alongside the playing area. The rigid, sharp fencing allegedly lacked adequate protective padding. The impact tore Gelof's uniform and caused a deep laceration beneath his right kneecap, narrowly missing his patellar tendon, according to the suit. He was removed from the game and missed 30 days of practices and games while recovering. Gelof alleges that the injury affected his statistics, career progression and earning potential, while leaving him at risk of reinjury. The lawsuit contends the defendants failed to maintain a reasonably safe playing environment and seeks compensation for Gelof's medical expenses, lost wages and career opportunities, plus pain and suffering. It does not specify a dollar amount but requests damages sufficient to “fully and fairly compensate him.” The lawsuit also notes that the Tigers installed protective padding over the exposed fencing shortly after the incident. mreinhart@detroitnews.com This article originally appeared on The Detroit News: Tigers respond to Gelof injury lawsuit in court. item.title: Bartlett High School football team moves on to playoffs, wins in honor of former teammate
item.description: The Bartlett High School football team made their way to Baldwinsville Friday night to take on Narragansett Regional High School. Aside from being a playoff-clinching game, the Bartlett Indians were playing for a greater purpose, honoring their former teammate. 18-year-old Francois Longdaye , of Webster, was one of three servicemen killed in a single-car crash last weekend in Pensacola, Florida. Longdaye was in Florida serving as a recruit for the Navy. ‘He’s everything to me’: Family, friends of fallen Navy sailor speak out after tragic loss Longdaye was a beloved member of the Bartlett High School football team and school community. He graduated earlier this year. Dane Laboissonniere, head coach of the football team, said it’s been a tough week for his team and coaching staff since they heard what happened. “It’s been a challenging week, and the kids are playing with heavy hearts,” Laboissonniere said. “To hear that news it was kind of unbelievable; it was definitely hard the first couple of days, and even now it’s still hard,” Tyler Whiting, a senior football player, said. “I was just heartbroken. I didn’t expect to hear that at all, and it’s just been tough,” Cameron Hast, a senior football player, said. This week, the team’s focus has been on supporting each other. “It’s been hard for all of us; we’ve all had to take mental timeouts, and we needed to take breaks every once in a while,” Jaesean Atkins, a junior football player, said. Laboissonniere said Longdaye was a former tight end and defensive lineman who played every play like it was his last. “He just played so hard, we used him as an example even after he graduated. We said, ' Look how hard he played on this play, played from whistle to whistle,’ Laboissonniere said. “He was a guy that was always there to hype everyone up; whenever you needed something, he was there,” Mast said. “He was a really good player… he had a lot of heart in everything he did,” Atkins said. His teammates and coach said Longdaye’s true character came through even beyond the field. “He always lifted everyone up, even when they’re down, even if you messed up one rep, one little thing, he was there making sure you’re ok and just being a great person overall.” The team poured their hearts into Friday night’s game, repping Longdaye’s #34 on their helmets and sweatshirts. Despite being a close game, the Indians rallied in the second half pulling off a win 38-20. They could be heard chanting “34” and “Franny” as they celebrated their win and moving on to the playoffs. “Everything we do is for him now… he’s always inside our hearts, he’s always with us,” Atkins said. item.title: Could Padres Reach Deals With Key Free Agents Soon?
item.description: San Diego Padres first baseman Ty France (25) hits an RBI single during the seventh inning of their National League Division Series game against the Milwaukee Brewers Sunday, October 4, 2026, at American Family Field in Milwaukee, Wiscon… | Source: Lastwordonsports.com - Augustus Oswald, Site Editor Sunday, November 1 marks the deadline for teams to decide whether to extend eligible impending free agents a qualifying offer or not. It’s also the time in which free agents are able to begin negotiating with other clubs. Until then, players may only negotiate internally with their own teams to potentially be re-signed. For the San Diego Padres, that represents a realm of possibilities. With several key free agents potentially leaving the club this offseason, the Friars could use this time to lock up some potential departures before they hit the open market. Here are four players who San Diego might reach deals with ahead of Sunday’s deadline. Could Padres Reach Deals With Key Free Agents Soon? 1B Ty France France surged at the plate this season, putting up career-best numbers in batting average (.295), slugging percentage (.502), OPS (.865), and home runs (21). After being drafted by the Padres in 2015, 2026 was a bit of a reunion tour for the slugger. San Diego would certainly like to extend that reunion, for the right price. France is projected to land a three-year, $49.3 million contract. That puts him at a $16.4 million average annual value (AAV), which is maybe a hair outside of San Diego’s comfort range. Oct 4, 2026; Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA; San Diego Padres first baseman Ty France (25) hits a single during the first inning against the Milwaukee Brewers in game two of the NLDS for the 2026 MLB Playoffs at American Family Field. Mandatory Credit: Benny Sieu-Imagn Images Still, France truly had a resurgent 2026 campaign. Not re-signing him would be a blunder of epic proportions. If nothing else, France plays near-perfect defense at the cold corner. He was named a Gold Glove finalist a few weeks ago and could win the award over Atlanta Braves first baseman Matt Olson . Regardless, there is a question about whether his incredible offensive production will continue into 2027 and beyond. That might stall a deal between the two sides. RHP Michael King This one is the least likely of the bunch. San Diego’s ace declined his $28 million player option on Thursday morning, meaning King is now a full-fledged free agent. He’ll probably test the open market to some extent. King is projected to land a five-year, $118 million deal this offseason after an incredible 2026 campaign (3.21 ERA, 185.0 IP). King’s postseason heroics with San Diego (0.64 ERA, 14.0 IP) make him even more desirable to the Padres and other contenders this offseason. item.description: New Jersey Devils center Jack Hughes and Vegas Golden Knights right wing Mark Stone (61) eye the puck during second period of NHL game against Vegas Golden Knights on Friday October 30, 2026 at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas. LAS VEGAS — If your name happened to be “Hughes,” Friday was a pretty good day. At Keeneland in Lexington, Kentucky, a 2-year-old colt named Hughes won the Breeders’ Cup Juvenile and with it, favoritism status for next year’s Kentucky Derby. At T-Mobile Arena, the Hughes brothers, Jack and Luke, dominated in leading the New Jersey Devils past the Vegas Golden Knights, 5-2. Jack, who had a pair of goals, probably should have had a hat trick, getting robbed by Adin Hill in the second period. Luke opened the scoring for New Jersey, which had Connor Hellebuyck in net for the second time after trading for the Olympic gold medalist last week in a blockbuster deal with the Winnipeg Jets. But on a day where Hill was once again very good and at times, spectacular, the guys in front of him were unable to match New Jersey as Arseny Gritsyuk joined the Hughes boys as a hero with a pair of goals. The top line for New Jersey had four goals and five points total. “We didn’t do a good enough job against them,” said Ivan Barbashev, who had the goal that briefly put Vegas in the lead. “We started turning the puck over and gave them everything they wanted to do. We have to play better.” The loss, Vegas’ fourth in its last five contests, stifled whatever momentum the team had generated from Tuesday’s 4-1 win over Ottawa. The Knights now head to Boston to face the Bruins Monday to start a four-games-in-seven-days East Coast road trip that includes a back-to-back in Pittsburgh Tuesday night along with games in Detroit next Thursday and concluding in Buffalo a week from Sunday. “We didn’t help ourselves,” Knights coach Ryan Craig said. New Jersey is a good team and they’re going to capitalize on your mistakes. But it starts with our puck play and turnovers. We didn’t check well enough and we just have to be better.” The Knights failed to sustain any offensive firepower against New Jersey, a team that is looking to stay within shooting distance of first-place Carolina in the Metropolitan Division. item.description: PISCATAWAY, N.J. — Maryland came to Yurcak Field without a road win all season. Rutgers put 18 shots on target against the Terrapins, and lost. The Terrapins beat the Scarlet Knights 3-2 on Friday night in the last match of both teams’ seasons. Jolie Farmer scored at 7:06 and again at 51:47, and Mia Mitchell converted a penalty at 38:43 after a handball on Sophia Stiles. Lilia Calvert answered from the spot at 56:25 and Reilly McGlinn made it 3-2 at 81:49 off a Julia Joseph assist, but the equalizer never came. Luckey made 13 saves before giving way to Meredith Fisher at 78:42, and Fisher made three more. Olivia Bodmer made one. Thirty-three shots. Eighteen on target. Two goals, and one of them from the spot. It was Halloween on the Pitch at Yurcak, with trick-or-treat bags and light sticks on the giveaway list for an announced crowd of 503, and it did not feel much like a holiday by the end. There was no postseason waiting. Rutgers’ Big Ten Tournament hopes were gone before kickoff, so the final whistle was the end of the year, and for five seniors the last match of their Rutgers careers. The mood on the Rutgers side afterward was somber, and plenty of players were emotional. Rutgers had come in off their best result of October. Sunday’s 4-0 win at Indiana ended a run of three straight matches without a goal, and McGlinn scored twice in it, her first goals of the season. Picked 15th of 18 in the Big Ten preseason poll, this team spent most of the fall looking better than its record. It beat No. 14 Wisconsin 3-1 on Senior Day, beat Northwestern on the Pink Out, and lost one-goal matches to Purdue, UCLA and Penn State. The finishing never fully caught up, and Friday was its last chance to. Maryland arrived 4-10-3 overall and 1-8-2 in the Big Ten, picked 17th in the preseason poll in Michael Marchiano’s second full season in charge. Its only conference win came Oct. 11 against Northwestern, it had been outscored 26-11, and it was 0-5-2 away from College Park. The senior goalkeeper came in with 71 saves in 14 starts and had just been named the department’s Terp of the Week. The series had gone to two straight draws, 1-1 at Yurcak on Senior Day in 2024 and 0-0 at Ludwig Field last October, when Rutgers outshot Maryland 19-7 and could not score. Maryland had won three of its seven previous trips to Piscataway. Maryland had not won on the road all year. It waited for the last night of Rutgers’ season. item.title: Carter Rye, Pickford football top Mio, reach MHSAA 8-player regional final
item.description: PICKFORD — Another regional semifinal, another win for the Pickford Panthers . Behind an excellent offensive display from senior quarterback Carter Rye , the Panthers advanced to their fourth consecutive MHSAA 8-Player Division 1 football regional final by rolling to a 40-12 victory over Mio on Friday, Oct. 30. Here's some takeaways from Friday's clash. Rye, Pickford offense unstoppable all night On the opening snap from scrimmage, it was clear that the Panthers (8-2) wanted to set the tone with their rushing attack, as Rye used several powerful runs to push Pickford deep into Mio territory. Despite facing a fourth-and-10, Rye hooked up with Carter Yiirs on a 10-yard touchdown pass that allowed the Panthers to take a 6-0 lead four minutes in. FOOTBALL THOUGHTS: Cheboygan-area teams miss out on playoffs, Pickford draws No. 1 seed PLAYOFF PAIRINGS: Inland Lakes misses playoffs; Pickford to host Mio in first round PICKFORD, INLAND LAKES THRILLER: Pickford holds on for thrilling 2OT victory over Inland Lakes From that point on, Pickford's offense couldn't be stopped as Rye broke loose for a 31-yard TD to help extend the Panthers' lead to 14-0. Rye added two more rushing scores in the second quarter, which helped Pickford build a commanding 26-0 halftime lead. Pickford continued its dominance in the third, capping another drive with a 4-yard TD run from Mason Andrzejak, while a successful 2-point conversion made it 34-0. Rye added another TD run with 5:04 left. Some things to clean up Overall, it was a dominant night for the Panthers. However, numerous penalties were committed on offensive possessions. While it wasn't really a problem Friday, it will be something Pickford will need to clean up if it wants to make another deep postseason run this fall. At times, Mio quarterback Cory Fox tested the Panthers with his arm, completing several deep passes. However, the Thunderbolts (6-4) struggled to find the end zone as the Panthers' defense rose to the occasion several times, with Rye picking off a pass that halted a Mio drive in the third. Mio finally got on the board with a touchdown midway through the fourth, while Fox tossed a TD pass late. U.P. regional final next Friday With Pickford's victory, the Panthers will have an opportunity to earn the program's third regional title in four seasons if they can knock off Ishpeming (8-2), which rolled its way to a 36-14 semifinal victory at Rudyard. The No. 1-seeded Panthers will surely be tested against an Ishpeming team that should have loads of confidence, especially after winning convincingly in Rudyard. Pickford holds a 3-0 advantage in the all-time series against the Hematites, including a 44-6 regional final victory two years ago. item.title: Kentucky ends Missouri’s five-match winning streak with sweep
item.description: Missouri volleyball’s five-match winning streak came to an end Thursday night in Lexington, Kentucky, as the Tigers fell to Kentucky 3-0 at Historic Memorial Coliseum. The Wildcats (25-16, 29-27, 25-17) controlled much of the match offensively, hitting .327 as a team while holding Missouri to a .168 hitting percentage. Kentucky also finished with 54 kills compared to Missouri’s 29, creating a significant gap in offensive production. Missouri struggled to find consistent answers for Kentucky’s attack, particularly from outside hitters Morgan Gaerte and Brooklyn DeLeye. Gaerte led all players with 19 kills on 40 attempts, hitting .350. DeLeye added 16 kills while hitting .344 and recorded three service aces. The Tigers had opportunities to even the match in the second set but could not capitalize. After dropping the opening set 25-16, Missouri responded with its strongest offensive showing of the night, recording 14 kills and hitting .233. Missouri pushed Kentucky to extra points in the second set, but the Wildcats eventually secured a 29-27 victory to take a commanding 2-0 lead. The Tigers’ inability to close out the set proved costly, as Kentucky carried its momentum into the third. Kentucky dominated the final set, holding Missouri to five kills and five errors on 20 attempts. The Tigers finished the set with a .000 hitting percentage as the Wildcats hit .333 to close out the sweep. Paige Felder and Lydia Stahley led Missouri with six and seven kills, respectively. Grace O’Reilly and Kimani Johnson added five kills apiece, while Lauren Larkin contributed three kills without committing an error. Defensively, Ainoah Cruz led the Tigers with 14 digs, while setter Nina Mandovic recorded 14 assists. Missouri finished with 32 digs and six total blocks but struggled to slow Kentucky’s offensive production. Kentucky setter Kassie O’Brien distributed 43 assists as the Wildcats totaled 50 assists and 47 digs. The Wildcats also held a considerable advantage in sideout percentage, converting 75.8% of their opportunities compared to Missouri’s 58.4%. The loss snaps Missouri’s five-match winning streak and gives the Tigers a setback as they continue their SEC schedule. After building momentum during the winning stretch, Missouri will look to regroup and rediscover its offensive consistency following Thursday’s three-set defeat. Mizzou is now 13-9 on the year and play No. 6 Tennessee Sunday at Hearns.

item.description: Bayer Leverkusen ultra group demands end to its own club’s 50+1 exemption One of Bayer Leverkusen’s organized supporter groups has called for their own club to relinquish its longstanding exemption from German football’s 50+1 ownership rule. Independent supporters’ association Nordkurve12 has directly challenged Bayer AG to embrace meaningful fan participation and warned that attempts to defend the club’s special ownership status through legal action could further jeopardize the future of the rule. The remarkable intervention comes amid renewed pressure from German football’s organised supporter groups ahead of the Bundesliga’s December membership assembly. The nationwide Fanszenen Deutschlands alliance has demanded that the league eliminate existing exemptions and implement the recommendations issued by Germany’s Federal Cartel Office in August. For Leverkusen, however, the dispute has taken on a particularly unusual dimension. Supporters of one of the Bundesliga’s two remaining beneficiaries of historic corporate ownership exemptions are openly demanding that their own club be subjected to the same rules as its competitors. Nordkurve12 challenges Bayer AG over special ownership status As reported by Kicker , Nordkurve12 issued a clear demand that Leverkusen’s exemption should no longer continue. “What should apply to German football as a whole must also be the standard in Leverkusen,” the supporters’ association declared. “Should Bayer AG attempt to defend or expand its existing special status through legal action, this could further intensify the dispute over the future of the 50+1 rule.” The supporters’ demands extend beyond merely removing the historic exemption. As BILD reports , Nordkurve12 is also calling for transparency, genuine member participation, and a common framework that would subject Leverkusen to the same ownership principles as other German professional clubs. The association reportedly intends to discuss these demands with Leverkusen’s leadership in the coming week. The intervention is particularly significant given Bayer 04’s historic relationship with the pharmaceutical and chemical company from which it takes its name. Unlike most Bundesliga clubs, Leverkusen’s professional football operations are wholly controlled by a corporate parent. Unlike most Bundesliga clubs, Leverkusen’s professional football company is wholly owned by Bayer AG. Although supporters have avenues for representation, including an elected supporters’ council, they do not exercise the majority voting control over the professional football operation that the 50+1 rule ordinarily reserves for a member-controlled parent club. item.description: Image Credit:By Lorie Shaull - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0/Wikimedia Commons. Sophie Cunningham has weighed in on the WNBA's national anthem controversy, questioning why teams' pregame routines are drawing criticism now when they have been happening all season. The Indiana Fever guard discussed the issue during the October 28 episode of Theo Von's This Past Weekend podcast. She did not name the Atlanta Dream or Golden State Valkyries, the two Finals teams whose absence from the court during the anthem has attracted attention. The criticism has reached beyond basketball. Vice President JD Vance has accused teams of disrespecting the country. Cunningham's own team followed a different routine. Indiana and Minnesota were among the WNBA teams that remained on the floor during the anthem this season. Cunningham Explains Her Family's Connection to Military Service Cunningham told Von that members of her family had served in the military. She credited service members with protecting the freedoms that allow her to pursue her career and said she wants to acknowledge veterans and those currently serving whenever she can. "That doesn't mean that's where everyone stands and if it's right, wrong, whatever," she said, according to Complex . "I take a lot of pride of where I come from, and I'm proud to be an American citizen." The Teams' Anthem Routines Predate This Year's Finals According to The Associated Press , WNBA teams have been leaving the court before the anthem for at least six seasons. Some have done so to draw attention to social justice issues, while others use the time to continue preparing for games. The Valkyries told the AP that their locker-room routine has been consistent since the franchise began playing in 2025. Atlanta has also left the floor before the anthem for several years. The league's written rulebook calls for players, coaches and trainers to stand along the sidelines or foul line during the anthem. However, the WNBA suspended those protocols late in the 2017 season, allowing players and coaches to show support for victims of the white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Virginia. The AP reported that the league appeared to be leaving the decision to teams, although who has final authority remained unclear. The WNBA did not respond to the outlet's request for clarification for its October 20 report. The Finals will be decided on October 31 in San Francisco. Atlanta's 80-69 win over Golden State on October 29 tied the series at three games apiece and forced the WNBA's first Finals Game 7.
